sub: Named after “the opening” (sharḥ) of the chest in ayah 1
theme: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ in hard early days: Allah opened his chest, lifted his load and raised his name. With hardship comes ease, so turn to Allah in worship.
story: Revealed in Makkah, reportedly right after Ad-Ḍuḥā, in the same setting.
When the Prophet ﷺ began calling people to Islam, the same people who had honoured him turned on him with insults and mockery. The early days were very hard.
The surah reminds him of three gifts already given, promises ease with the hardship, and shows him where to find strength: worship and turning to Allah.

sections.title: Three gifts: his chest opened, his burden lifted, his name raised
sections.meaning: Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ of three gifts: He opened his chest wide, lifted the heavy load that weighed on his back, and raised his name high, so it is mentioned alongside Allah’s own.
points: Did We not open your chest?
We lifted the load that weighed down your back
sections.matters: When the people who once honoured him turned hostile, Allah reminded him what he had already been given. Each gift is said lak, “for you”: they were given for his sake.
sections.story: No specific incident. It came to comfort the Prophet ﷺ when the people around him turned hostile after he began to preach.
explained: Sharḥ aṣ-ṣadr: Allah filled his chest with light, faith and wisdom, and made it wide enough to carry the message. Some link it to the angels opening his chest. His wizr, the load that almost broke his back, is either past slips forgiven, or the weight of prophethood made lighter.
Rafaʿnā laka dhikrak: whenever Allah is mentioned, he is mentioned with Him: in the shahādah, the adhān, the iqāmah, the tashahhud in prayer and in sermons. No other person is praised like this.
teaches: An open, wide heart is a gift from Allah.
Allah lightens loads that feel back-breaking.
Real honour comes from Allah, not from people.
sections.hook: Three gifts, each with lak or ʿanka, “for you” or “from you”, and every ayah ends in -ka: ṣadrak, wizrak, ẓahrak, dhikrak.

sections.title: With hardship comes ease; when free, strive in worship toward your Lord
sections.meaning: With hardship comes ease, and it is said twice. So when you finish your work, stand and tire yourself in worship, and turn all your longing to your Lord alone.
points: With hardship comes ease; with hardship comes ease
When you are free, strive in worship
And to your Lord alone turn your longing
sections.matters: It is a promise for every believer, not only for that moment. And it shows how to carry hardship: when the day’s work is done, turn fully to Allah.
sections.story: Reportedly Quraysh mocked the Prophet ﷺ for being poor and offered to collect money for him. He was saddened, and Allah promised ease. When it came down he said: “Rejoice, one hardship will never overcome two eases.”
explained: Al-ʿusr, the hardship, comes with “the”, so both ayat speak of the same hardship. Yusr, ease, comes without “the”, so there are two eases. One hardship will never defeat two. And ease does not only follow hardship; it comes maʿa, with it.

Fa-idhā faraghta fa-nṣab: when you finish your duties, whether work, teaching or the obligatory prayer, tire yourself in worship and duʿāʾ. Wa ilā rabbika fa-rghab: make your Lord alone the object of your hope.
teaches: No hardship comes without ease beside it.
One hardship can’t beat two eases.
Use free time for worship, not idleness.
Put your hope in Allah alone.
sections.hook: Ayat 5 and 6 are identical except for the fa- that opens 5. The surah ends with two short commands: fa-nṣab (7) and fa-rghab (8).

groups.text: Did We not open your chest wide for you?
We lifted from you the heavy load that weighed down your back.
And We raised your name high.
With hardship comes ease; truly, with hardship comes ease.
When you are free, strive in worship, and turn your longing to your Lord.

1.explain: A lam nashraḥ: of course We opened your chest, filling it with light, faith, knowledge and wisdom, and making it wide and at ease. The question makes him affirm it.

2.explain: Wa waḍaʿnā ʿanka wizrak: We lifted your burden. Either past slips, now forgiven, or the heavy weight of carrying prophethood, made easier.

3.explain: Anqaḍa ẓahrak: a load so heavy it bent his back until it almost creaked.

4.explain: Rafaʿnā laka dhikrak: whenever Allah is mentioned, you are mentioned with Him, in the shahādah, adhān, iqāmah, tashahhud and sermons.

5.explain: Fa-inna maʿa-l-ʿusri yusrā: with the hardship comes ease, not just after it. For the Prophet ﷺ, the hardship he suffered from the disbelievers turned into victory.
5.why: Reportedly Quraysh taunted the Prophet ﷺ for being poor and offered to collect wealth to make him rich. He was saddened, thinking they rejected him for his poverty, so Allah listed His favours and promised ease.

6.explain: Repeated to confirm the promise. Al-ʿusr, with “the”, is the same hardship; yusr, without it, is a second ease. So one hardship will never overcome two eases.

7.explain: Fa-idhā faraghta fa-nṣab: when you are free from your tasks, or finish the obligatory prayer, tire yourself in worship and duʿāʾ. Another view: stand in night prayer.

8.explain: Fa-rghab: turn your longing and hope to your Lord alone, asking Him humbly, fearing the Fire and hoping for Paradise.
